{{Short description|Property of mathematical sets}}
In [[mathematics]], a '''cocountable''' [[subset]] of a set <math> X </math> is a subset <math> Y </math> whose [[complement (set theory)|complement]] in <math> X </math> is a [[countable set]]. In other words, <math> Y </math> contains all but countably many elements of <math> X </math>. Since the rational numbers are a countable subset of the reals, for example, the irrational numbers are a cocountable subset of the reals. If the complement is finite, then one says <math> Y </math> is [[cofinite]].{{r|halgiv}}

== σ-algebras ==

The set of all subsets of <math> X </math> that are either countable or cocountable forms a [[sigma-algebra|σ-algebra]], i.e., it is closed under the operations of countable unions, countable intersections, and complementation. This σ-algebra is the ''countable-cocountable algebra'' on <math> X </math>. It is the smallest σ-algebra containing every [[singleton set]].{{r|sigma}}

== Topology ==

The [[cocountable topology]] (also called the "countable complement topology") on any set <math> X </math> consists of the [[empty set]] and all cocountable subsets of <math> X </math>.{{r|james}}
